summary:
Imagine‍‍‍ being on Mars. Your oxygen is almost gone. There's a steep, dangerous slope right ahead, and you can't know exactly where you are in this vast rocky landscape. On top of that, if you could call home, the signal would take 20 minutes to reach Earth.
We wanted to help spacewalkers out of this kind of nightmare. And so we created one to help walk on Mars. Introducing Oxydia, a Raspberry Pi-powered wrist device that’s not only a 3D map but also a space guide and smart,”walk on the spot” Way
We partnered with NASA by using their real Mars rover data with pics of the surface to bring the Red Planet close to your wrist. We made the maps with a cool 3D map of Mars with pics of the surface that had over a hundred meters of difference from what the rovers were doing. And we fixed it. Now we can locate you at a few meters, as if we had GPS on Mars.
It’s like satellite navigation for the ground: Oxydia guides you around steep slopes, will see if spots are one way, listen for rocks and other smart things with a camera hooked to AI. We're working on adding the toughest paths and testing new ways to learn from the experience and help you get safely across the surface of Mars, and one day, this device could be helping us humans explore a new ‍‍‍planet.
details:
What‍‍‍ it does

Oxydia is a navigation device worn on the wrist by an astronaut walking on Mars. It displays a full map of the planet, includes a real-time safe route planning algorithm, and surveys the planet using a camera. It functions in offline mode: Mars has no GPS, and the average time for a response from Earth is roughly twenty minutes.

How it works

- Map: on the one hand, we mapped Mars using public data with some additional resolution on eight interesting places to explore (like Jezero and Gale) and 3D with 1 m resolution on four of those eight places.

- Accuracy: we discovered that the maps made from public photos and altimetry data were not perfectly aligned and the misalignment was up to 50 100 m. We found a way to correct that and to be confident up to a few meters for the position of the rover: From 50 100 m down to 3 6 m.

- Route: our A* planner does not allow slopes over 25° and keeps a safe distance to the obstacles. It is smart enough to provide a route in less than half a second.

- AI camera: we trained a model with thousands of real rover pictures identifying rocks, and so far, we have not encountered a false positive. When a specific rock is detected in the shot, it is automatically turned into a hazard, and a new route is calculated.

- Field tools: a large, glove friendly buttons interface, geotagging photos for later science documentation, a part with a checklist for the rover, weather data coming from Curiosity, and even an alert for dust storms.

Benefits and impact

This way, the astronauts have the time to do the science instead of waiting for mission control: safer walks and more time to actually explore. And if the technology is good enough for Mars, why not the Moon or isolated places on Earth?

Tools

Hardware: Raspberry Pi CM5, touchscreen, Sony IMX500 AI camera.

Software: written in Python (GDAL, NumPy, ONNX Runtime, Flask, Tkinter), plus JavaScript with MapLibre GL and Electron. (Ben used Claude as a coding assistant)

What makes it creative

Usually, Mars maps show the entire area from the orbital aspect. But we are talking about a man on a mission who has to visit a location like this so we engaged the movement of the man with the inertial rover movement, and the ground-attached camera on the field.

What we considered

Safety first, usability with gloves, a small computer that heats up in the Sun, and honesty: the AI is weaker on rocks, and the device says ‍‍‍so.
